explanation: Double-quoted strings interpolate variables and interpret escape sequences (e.g. \n, \t), while single-quoted strings treat content almost literally; the difference is not merely speed.
The null coalescing operator (??) is shorthand for isset() ?: and does not raise warnings or notices for undefined variables.
The echo statement in PHP accepts multiple comma-separated arguments and prints them consecutively without any separator.
In PHP, print is a language construct that evaluates to the string '1', so it can be used inside expressions (unlike echo).
The Elvis operator returns the left operand when it is truthy, and the right operand when it is falsy.
In PHP, the concatenation operator (.) has lower precedence than arithmetic operators like + and -, so 'a + b . c' is parsed as '(a + b) . c'.
The ** operator is right-associative in PHP, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512, not 64.
The + operator has higher precedence than the . concatenation operator, so it is parsed as 'sum: ' . (2 + 3) = 'sum: 5'.
With strict comparison (===), arrays must have the same key/value pairs in the same order and be of the same type to be considered equal.
0 == false returns true (not false), and == is a loose comparison, not a strict one (=== is strict).
In PHP 8, when comparing a non-numeric string to an integer, the integer is cast to a string instead, so 'abc' == 0 becomes 'abc' == '0', which is false.
In PHP (prior to 8.0), null == 0, null == '', and null == false all evaluate to true under loose comparison.
Casting a string to int in PHP parses the leading numeric portion, so '42abc' becomes 42.
PHP coerces the numeric string '5' to an integer and performs arithmetic addition, resulting in the integer 10.
Casting false to a string in PHP results in an empty string "", not "0".
Due to floating-point precision, 0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.30000000000000004, which is not strictly equal (===) to 0.3.
strrev() reverses a string byte-by-byte, which corrupts multi-byte UTF-8 characters; use mb_strrev() instead.
str_contains() returns true because 'world' is found as a substring in 'Hello world'.
str_pad() can pad on the left (STR_PAD_LEFT), right (STR_PAD_RIGHT), or both sides (STR_PAD_BOTH).
By default, trim() strips spaces, tabs, newlines, returns, nulls, and vertical tabs — not just spaces.
In UTF-8, 'h'=1 byte, 'é'=2 bytes (U+00E9 → 0xC3A9), 'l'=1, 'l'=1, 'o'=1, totaling 6 bytes.
substr with a negative start position of -3 begins 3 characters from the end of 'abcdef', returning 'def'.
ucfirst() returns a new string with the first character uppercased; it does not modify the original string in place.
Heredoc (<<EOF) interpolates variables like double-quoted strings, while nowdoc (<<<'EOF') treats content as a single-quoted string with no interpolation.
sort() re-indexes the array with numeric keys; asort() is the function that preserves key-to-value association.
In PHP, string keys that represent valid integers are automatically cast to integer keys, so '5' is stored as the integer 5.
in_array() uses loose comparison (==) by default; the third parameter $strict must be explicitly set to true to use ===.
Without a callback, array_filter() removes elements that evaluate to falsy (false, 0, '', '0', null, []) by default.
By default, the $preserve_keys parameter is false, so array_slice() reindexes the resulting array starting from 0.
array_slice starts at index 1 and takes 2 elements, yielding [20, 30].
Array union keeps left-side values for duplicate keys and only adds new keys from the right side, resulting in ['a'=>1, 'b'=>2'].
PHP 8.1 extended the array spread operator to allow arrays with string keys, previously it only worked with integer keys.
Named arguments can be combined with argument unpacking in a single call, as long as the named arguments come before the ...$args unpacking (e.g., func(a: 1, ...$args) is valid).
In PHP, closures do not automatically inherit outer scope variables; you must explicitly use the 'use' keyword to import them.
func_num_args() returns the number of arguments passed to the function call, which is 3 (1, 2, 3), regardless of how many parameters are declared.
Arrow functions (fn) in PHP are limited to a single expression body; they cannot use curly braces with multiple statements.
PHP arrow functions (fn) capture outer variables by value at the time of creation, not by reference at use time.
In PHP, a static closure does not bind to the object scope, so $this is not available inside it.
The closure captures $x by value at creation time (5), so the later reassignment to 7 does not affect it.
In coercive (weak) typing mode, PHP automatically converts compatible values like the string '5' to the expected int type.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing properties to be declared and assigned directly in the constructor parameters.
The 'final' keyword in PHP prevents a method from being overridden by subclasses.
In PHP, a final method cannot be overridden in a subclass; attempting to do so results in a fatal error.
Private properties are only accessible within the class that defines them, not in subclasses.
Anonymous classes in PHP have a generated name where the part before the NUL byte is 'Class@anonymous'.
A private method in the parent class is not visible to the child, so the child is free to declare a method with the same name using any visibility (public, protected, or private).
__get() is called for both inaccessible (private/protected) and undefined properties when accessed from outside the class.
Reassigning a readonly property in PHP 8.1+ throws an Error (not an Exception).
In PHP, interfaces can declare constants, which are always public and cannot be overridden by implementing classes.
The instanceof operator in PHP checks whether an object is an instance of a specific class or interface.
PHP interfaces can declare static methods, and the implementing class must provide the static method implementation.
PHP's instanceof operator checks both class inheritance and interface implementation, so an object is instanceof an interface if its class implements that interface.
PHP interface methods must be abstract and cannot have a body; only traits (and regular classes) can provide default method implementations.
In PHP, abstract methods can be declared as public or protected, so protected visibility is allowed.
Foo::cases() returns an array of all enum cases, and there are three: A, B, and C.
Traits in PHP can declare constants, which are then accessible in any class that uses the trait.
In PHP 7+, both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface, making it their common ancestor.
TypeError extends Error, not Exception; they are sibling classes both implementing Throwable, so catch(Exception) will not catch TypeError.
The @ operator suppresses errors (warnings, notices) but does not suppress exceptions; exceptions will still be thrown and must be handled with try/catch.
intdiv(5, 0) throws a DivisionByZeroError because the divisor is zero.
The finally block runs regardless of whether an exception was thrown or caught; it always executes.
An exception thrown in a finally block will actually suppress (replace) any exception that was thrown in the try block, so it does have an effect.
In PHP, casting any object to bool always results in true, so (bool) new Exception('x') evaluates to true (yes).
Shutdown functions registered with register_shutdown_function() are called during the shutdown process, which is triggered when exit() or die() is called.
The use statement is a compile-time alias that simply maps a shorter name to a fully qualified class name; it does not trigger autoloading or load the file.
In PHP, 'use function' is used to import a function from a namespace, while 'use const' is used to import a constant.
PSR-4 strips the 'App\' prefix, converts remaining namespace separators to directory slashes, and appends .php, giving src/Controller/Api/UserController.php.
Composer's vendor/autoload.php ultimately creates a ClassLoader instance and registers it via spl_autoload_register().
__NAMESPACE__ is a PHP magic constant that is compiled at build time and contains the name of the current namespace (or an empty string for the global namespace).
An unqualified class name in `new` is resolved relative to the current namespace, not the global root; a leading backslash is required to force global resolution.
PSR-4 maps the remaining namespace segments (Model\User) to subdirectories and filename, resulting in src/Model/User.php.
In PHP, a use statement can be placed inside a function body, in which case the imported alias is scoped to that function only.
In PHP, arrays are value types and are copied on assignment (using copy-on-write optimization since PHP 5.3), not passed by reference by default.
PHP arrays are copied by value (copy-on-write), so modifying $b does not affect $a, which still has 2 elements.
In PHP, variables in the global scope are not visible inside function scope unless explicitly accessed via the global keyword, $GLOBALS superglobal, or passed as parameters.
$GLOBALS['x'] is a direct reference to the global variable, so unset($GLOBALS['x']) removes the global variable entirely, not just for the current function scope.
The function takes $x by reference, so incrementing $x inside the function modifies $n directly, resulting in 6.
PHP's foreach (by value) iterates over the array's internal structure as it exists at loop start; newly added elements are not visited in the same pass, and removals can cause elements to be skipped.
A static property belongs to the class itself, not to individual instances, so all objects share the same value and changes are visible across all instances.
In PHP, boolean array keys are cast to integers: true becomes 1 and false becomes 0, so they are stored as int, not bool.
Since PHP 7.1, a generator can return a value (not yield it), and that value is accessible via the Generator::getReturn() method after the generator is fully consumed.
PHP generators are one-shot iterators; once fully consumed, they cannot be rewound or traversed again.
The yield from construct (a Python feature) does delegate traversal to another generator or iterable, making the statement true.
A function containing yield returns a Generator object, and get_class() returns its class name 'Generator'.
The generator yields 3 elements (1, 2, 3) via yield from, iterator_to_array converts them to an array of 3 elements, and count returns 3.
SplStack implements a LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) stack, not a FIFO queue; SplQueue is the class that implements a FIFO queue.
ArrayIterator is a built-in PHP class that wraps an array and implements the Iterator interface, allowing traversal via current(), key(), next(), rewind(), and valid() methods.
ArrayObject implements the Iterator interface, so it can be traversed with foreach.
password_hash() automatically generates and embeds a random salt in the returned hash; there is no salt parameter to pass.
In PHP 8, PASSWORD_DEFAULT is Argon2id, not MD5.
password_verify() returns true when the plaintext password matches the given hash, which it does here since the hash was generated from the same string 'secret'.
strip_tags() removes HTML/PHP tags and has no role in preventing SQL injection; that requires prepared statements or proper escaping.
session_regenerate_id() creates a new session ID, invalidating the old one, which is the standard defense against session fixation attacks, especially upon privilege changes like login.
php_sapi_name() returns the SAPI name, such as 'cli' for command-line interface.
session_destroy() only destroys the session data on the server; the session cookie in the browser must be explicitly cleared with setcookie() or a header.
session_start() must be called before $_SESSION is available; it is not automatically populated without it.
array_find() is not a built-in PHP function; no such function exists in PHP's standard library.
PHP 8.4 introduced property hooks, allowing get/set logic to be defined directly in the property declaration.
Asymmetric visibility (e.g., public private(set) string $name) is a new feature introduced in PHP 8.4.
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.4 to indicate that a function's return value should not be silently discarded.
The pipe operator |> has been proposed in PHP RFCs but has not been accepted or released in any PHP version as of PHP 8.4.
The 'clone-with' syntax clone($obj, ['x' => 1]) does not exist in any released PHP version; PHP's clone keyword only supports the simple clone $object form.
array_first() and array_last() are not built-in PHP functions in any released version as of PHP 8.4; they are commonly found in frameworks like Laravel but are not part of the standard PHP library.
There is no RFC called 'Partial Function Application v2' in PHP; this appears to be a fabricated RFC name.
The clamp() function was introduced in PHP 8.4 via the accepted RFC clamp_v2.
The Context Managers v2 RFC has not been adopted into PHP; it was rejected or remains unaccepted as of the stated date.
The Bound-Erased Generic Types RFC was declined in 2025, not 2026.
As of the current date, no RFC enabling ZTS (Zend Thread Safety) multithreading by default has been accepted in PHP; the default build remains non-thread-safe.
PHP has never implemented true generics (parameterized types), and no such feature exists in PHP 8.5 or any prior version.
PHP follows a yearly November release cycle, so PHP 8.5 (released Nov 2025) would be the latest stable as of Nov 7, 2026, with PHP 8.6's GA expected around Nov 19, 2026.
PHP 6 was planned but never released; PHP 7.0 (December 2015) followed directly after the PHP 5.6 series.
The RFC to add a built-in #[\Deprecated] attribute to PHP core was not adopted; deprecation is still handled via E_DEPRECATED notices and @deprecated docblocks.
In clean and onion architecture, the dependency rule dictates that all dependencies point inward toward the domain core, so inner layers have no knowledge of outer ones.

In DDD and clean architecture, domain entities are pure PHP objects that should have no dependencies on frameworks like Symfony or ORMs like Doctrine, keeping the domain layer decoupled from infrastructure.
Controllers and Twig templates belong to the presentation (interface) layer, not the business-logic layer; they call use cases but are not themselves business logic.
In onion architecture, the domain layer (entities and business rules) sits at the very center, with all other layers depending inward toward it.
Deptrac is a PHP layer-dependency analyzer that enforces architectural rules and fails the build when a forbidden layer dependency is detected.

Use cases (interactors) should be framework-agnostic and infrastructure-agnostic; accepting an HTTP request or EntityManager couples them to specific technologies, violating Clean Architecture principles.
The Repository pattern provides a collection-like interface for accessing domain aggregates/entities while abstracting the underlying storage mechanism.

In Clean Architecture the database is an outermost-layer detail; the domain and use cases depend only on interfaces (ports), so swapping the DB engine requires changes only in the frameworks/drivers layer.

An aggregate is a domain-level consistency boundary (a cluster of entities and value objects), not a technical storage structure like a database table; they exist at different layers of the architecture and do not necessarily map one-to-one.
Value Objects are immutable and their equality is determined by the values of their fields, not by object identity (reference equality).
In Domain-Driven Design, the Aggregate Root is the single entry point of an aggregate through which all external modifications must pass.
In DDD, a repository is defined for an aggregate root, and all entities within that aggregate are accessed through the root, not via their own repositories.
In Domain-Driven Design, Ubiquitous Language is the shared vocabulary used consistently by both developers and domain experts to describe the domain model.
In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context is the boundary within which a model and its ubiquitous language are consistent, while the same terms may mean different things outside it.
DDD recommends rich domain models where business logic is encapsulated within the domain objects themselves; anemic models with logic in services are considered an anti-pattern in DDD.

In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context is a boundary within which a domain model applies, and the same real-world concept can be modeled as different classes with different attributes and behaviors in different contexts.
Symfony's DI container instantiates services only when they are first requested (e.g., via get() or injection), not eagerly at container build time.
The Symfony console command 'debug:router' lists all registered routes in the application.
The whole purpose of autowiring is to automatically resolve dependencies based on type hints, eliminating the need to manually declare most services in services.yaml.
Twig compiles templates into PHP classes (extending Twig\Template) and caches the resulting PHP files to avoid recompilation on subsequent requests.
In the dev environment, Symfony caches the compiled container and only rebuilds it when tracked files (e.g., service config, kernel) have changed.
Since Symfony 4.4/5.x, the APP_ENV environment variable determines the active environment (e.g., dev, prod, test).
Symfony controller action methods must be public; the framework invokes them via reflection and will throw an error if the method is private.
Both listeners and subscribers are ordered by priority value, not by their type; a subscriber with low priority will be called after a listener with high priority.
The Guard authentication system was removed in Symfony 6.0, and the new system is based on AuthenticatorInterface (introduced in 5.3).
The #[IsGranted] attribute in Symfony checks if the current user has the specified role or permission on a controller method, returning a 403 Forbidden if they don't.
Voters in Symfony are the mechanism for object-level access control, and isGranted('EDIT', $post) is the typical way to check a specific permission on a specific object using the Voter system.
Symfony 7 removed support for the doctrine/annotations-based annotation syntax, so validation constraints must be declared using PHP 8 attributes like #[Assert\NotBlank].
Symfony forms have CSRF protection enabled by default; a token is automatically added and validated on submission unless explicitly disabled.
Symfony always performs server-side form validation; client-side HTML5 checks are only a UX convenience and can be bypassed, so server-side validation is mandatory.
The Symfony MakerBundle command 'make:form' generates a FormType class.
Symfony only stores the user's identity (e.g., user ID) in the session after authentication; the password is never stored in the session, as it is verified against a hash and then discarded.
In Symfony, bundle configurations are conventionally stored in config/packages/ with one file per bundle or topic (e.g., framework.yaml, doctrine.yaml, twig.yaml).
This is a common best practice: commit a .env with safe dev defaults for reference, while keeping actual secrets in a gitignored .env.local (or similar) file.
The Symfony command 'debug:container' lists all registered services and their aliases in the service container.
Once the container is frozen (which happens at kernel boot), calling setParameter() throws a LogicException; you can only get parameters, not set them, from a controller.
Since Symfony 4.0, services are private by default (public: false) to allow the container to optimize and remove unused services.
Many bundles work without any configuration file in config/packages, as they can rely on autoconfiguration or have sensible defaults built in.
In Symfony, environment variables are referenced in YAML configuration files (like services.yaml) using the %env(VAR)% syntax.
The APP_DEBUG environment variable in Symfony controls debug mode, enabling the profiler, Twig debug toolbar, and detailed error pages.
Symfony Messenger allows multiple handlers for a single message, which will all be executed in sequence.
The sync transport processes the message immediately in the same process without any queueing; it does not wait for a worker.
The Symfony console command `messenger:consume` starts the worker that processes messages from the Messenger queue transport.
In Symfony Messenger, the retry_strategy (max_retries, delay, multiplier, max_delay) is configured per transport in the framework configuration.
Symfony Messenger's default Serializer uses the Symfony Serializer component with 'json' as the default format.
Symfony Scheduler is designed to schedule the dispatching of messages through the Messenger component at defined times.
The 'doctrine' transport in Symfony Messenger stores messages in database tables managed by Doctrine ORM.
Laravel's Messenger allows you to extend its pipeline by adding custom middleware via the $middleware property on a command, which can be placed before or after built-in middleware.
Symfony major releases come out every year (not every two years), while minor releases do come every six months in May and November.
Symfony 8 requires a minimum PHP version of 8.4, following Symfony's pattern of requiring the latest stable PHP release.
Symfony 7.0 removed support for docblock annotations; PHP 8 attributes are now the only supported way to configure validation, routes, etc.
Symfony's AssetMapper component manages CSS/JS assets using an import map (importmap.php) without requiring Node.js or webpack.
Symfony 6.4 is a Long-Term Support (LTS) release, with bug fixes until November 2025 and security fixes until November 2027.
Symfony removes deprecated features in the next major version; that is the entire purpose of the deprecation cycle.
Symfony provides an UPGRADE-X.Y.md guide for each major release, documenting all breaking changes and migration steps.
Symfony AssetMapper (symfony/asset-mapper) is the component that manages assets and importmaps without requiring Node.js or Webpack.
Symfony releases minor versions roughly every 6 months; as of November 2026, at most Symfony 8.0 or 8.1 could be out, making 8.2 not yet released.
Following the six-month cycle from Symfony 7.0 (May 2024), version 8.2 would land around November 2027, not November 2026 (which would correspond to ~8.0).
Following Symfony's semver minor release cadence, the version after 8.1 is 8.2.
Symfony major releases introduce breaking changes requiring migration work, but not a full rewrite, and '8.2' would be a minor release within the 8.x line, not a major one.

PHP's backward compatibility policy guarantees that within the same major version (e.g., 8.1 → 8.2), existing code will not be broken; only new features are added and deprecations may be introduced without removal.
Following Symfony's pattern of five minor releases per major branch (like 5.4 and 6.4), the last minor version of the 8.x line before 9.0 is 8.4.
Symfony 8.2 does not exist; the current major line is Symfony 7.x, and no such version with a PHP 8.5 requirement is documented.
Symfony's deprecation policy guarantees that deprecated features are only removed in the next major version, so deprecations introduced in 8.x will persist at least until 9.0.

Twig's {{ }} syntax only supports its own limited expression language (variables, filters, basic operators, method calls on objects) and does not allow calling arbitrary PHP functions or code directly.
Twig auto-escapes variables by default using the 'html' escaping strategy to prevent XSS attacks.
The |e filter (short for |escape) escapes a string for safe HTML output by default using htmlspecialchars.
The number_format filter from twig/intl-extra formats a number according to a given locale.
In Blade templates, the |raw filter prevents auto-escaping, allowing the value to be output as-is (equivalent to using {!! !!} syntax).
In Twig, {{ }} is used to output the value of an expression, while {% %} is used to execute structural tags like if, for, and set.
Twig allows declaring variables inside templates using the {% set %} tag.
The dump() function in Twig outputs the debug structure of a variable, similar to var_dump() in PHP.
Bootstrap is a front-end CSS/JS library providing UI components (grids, buttons, modals, etc.) and is not an SPA framework like React, Angular, or Vue.
The .container class in Bootstrap provides a responsive centered container with a fixed max-width at each breakpoint, unlike .container-fluid which is always 100% width.
The Bootstrap grid splits a row into 12 columns (not 16), and modern Bootstrap (v4+) uses Flexbox rather than CSS floats.
Bootstrap 5 defines exactly five named breakpoints: sm, md, lg, xl, and xxl.
In Bootstrap, spacing utilities like .mt-3 or .px-2 compute their value as the number multiplied by $spacer (e.g., 3 * $spacer).
In Bootstrap 5, the data-bs-toggle attribute is used to enable interactive components such as dropdowns, tooltips, popovers, and collapse on an element.
Bootstrap 5 removed its jQuery dependency and all components are built with vanilla JavaScript.
Bootstrap 5 dark mode is enabled with the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute, not a .dark class.
Doctrine ORM does not automatically create tables at runtime; you must explicitly run schema tools (e.g., orm:schema-tool:update) to create or update the database schema.
EntityManager::persist() marks an entity as managed and schedules an INSERT, but the SQL is only executed when flush() is called.
EntityManager::merge() exists in Doctrine ORM 3 and returns a managed copy of the passed detached entity.
DQL (Doctrine Query Language) is an ORM-level query language that uses entity names and their mapped fields rather than raw table and column names.
Doctrine's EntityRepository::find() returns null when no entity with the given ID is found.
By default, DoctrineBundle's auto_commit option is true, which causes flush() to be called automatically at the end of each request.
The Unit of Work tracks managed entities and detects property changes automatically, so flush() will generate the appropriate UPDATE query without needing an explicit persist() call.
Doctrine's remove() only schedules the deletion in the Unit of Work; the actual SQL DELETE is executed when flush() is called.
MVCC's purpose is precisely the opposite: readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers, as they operate on different versions of the data.
The EXPLAIN command displays the query execution plan without actually running the query.

While both auto-generate integers, SERIAL is a PostgreSQL shorthand that creates a separate sequence + default + unique constraint, whereas GENERATED AS IDENTITY is a SQL-standard column attribute with different management and behavior.
In PostgreSQL, NULL values are considered distinct from each other, so a UNIQUE constraint allows multiple rows with NULL in the same column.
PostgreSQL's string_agg() aggregate function concatenates strings with a specified separator.
Plain VACUUM only marks dead tuple space as reusable within the table; it does not return space to the operating system (that requires VACUUM FULL).
The PARTITION BY clause in a window function divides the result set into groups over which the window function is computed.
READ COMMITTED only prevents dirty reads; non-repeatable reads are prevented at the REPEATABLE READ level or higher.
By default, PostgreSQL runs in autocommit mode, where each SQL statement is automatically committed upon completion unless explicitly wrapped in a BEGIN...COMMIT block.
The COMMIT SQL command ends a transaction and permanently saves all changes made within it.
Indexes help the database engine quickly locate rows for any DML operation (SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE) that uses the indexed column in the WHERE clause.
SAVEPOINT allows you to create a named point within a transaction that you can roll back to, undoing only the statements after that point without aborting the entire transaction.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and reports real execution times, whereas plain EXPLAIN shows the plan without executing.
pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds a vector type and supports vector similarity indexing for embedding search.
A partial index in PostgreSQL contains only the rows that satisfy the specified WHERE condition, reducing index size and improving performance for targeted queries.
PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE using Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which relies on MVCC and anomaly detection/aborts, not by locking rows read by the transaction.
HTTP 201 'Created' indicates that the request was successful and a new resource was created as a result.
HTTP 204 No Content indicates a successful request with an empty response body, commonly returned after DELETE operations.
The HTTP specification (RFC 7231) explicitly classifies DELETE as an idempotent method, meaning repeated requests have the same effect on the server state.
The Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is sent by the server (not the client) to indicate which origin is permitted to access the resource.
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests is specifically defined (RFC 6585) for indicating that a client has sent too many requests in a given time frame, i.e., it has exceeded a rate limit.
It's the opposite: 4xx codes indicate client errors and 5xx codes indicate server errors.
The Content-Type HTTP header specifies the MIME type of the request or response body.
RFC 5789 explicitly states that PATCH is not idempotent by default, whereas PUT is required to be idempotent per RFC 7231.
Using == is vulnerable to timing attacks; you should use hash_equals() for constant-time comparison.
CSRF tokens are server-generated, bound to the session, and validated server-side on state-changing requests like POST, PUT, DELETE.
The Content-Security-Policy HTTP header is used to declare which resources are allowed to load on a page.

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization protocol, not an authentication protocol; it grants access to resources on behalf of a user without necessarily identifying who that user is (that's OpenID Connect's role).
XSS is primarily prevented by context-aware output encoding when rendering data in HTML, not by input validation before database storage.
In the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, the 'code' parameter is returned to the redirect_uri and then exchanged for an access token at the token endpoint.
Refresh tokens are designed to have a longer lifespan than access tokens and are used to obtain new access tokens without requiring the user to re-authenticate.
The salt does not need to be secret; it is typically stored alongside the hash (e.g., in bcrypt or argon2 output) and its purpose is uniqueness, not confidentiality.
PHPUnit requires test classes to extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase in order to be recognized and executed.
setUp() runs before each test method; setUpBeforeClass() (static) runs once before all tests.
A data provider allows a test to run with multiple sets of arguments, not just one.
The PHPUnit method expectException() declares an expectation that an exception of the given class will be thrown.
It's the opposite: a stub returns pre-programmed data, while a mock verifies which methods were called (and can also return data).
PHPUnit 10 deprecated the @dataProvider docblock annotation in favor of the #[DataProvider] PHP attribute.
PHPUnit supports test dependencies via the @depends annotation or depends() method, allowing one test to receive the result of another as a parameter.
PHPUnit's --order-by option accepts 'random' as a value to shuffle test execution order.
